node.label: Marisa J. Fuentes
node.description: Historian of slavery, gender and the Caribbean whose work asks what archival violence permits historians to know. Her 2010 abstract challenges triumphalist accounts of Rachael Pringle Polgreen by examining power over other women. The read excerpt from Dispossessed Lives (2016) explains the limits of recovering enslaved women’s perspectives and the need to change the archival gaze. With Deborah Gray White, Fuentes coedited the collective Scarlet and Black project at Rutgers. Her 2017 AAIHS essay connects this methodological problem with contemporary studies of slavery and capitalism and explicitly acknowledges Hartman’s essay as inspiration for a jointly edited project.
node.representative_figures_and_works: “Power and Historical Figuring” (2010); Dispossessed Lives (2016); with Deborah Gray White, editor, Scarlet and Black, Volume 1 (2016); with Brian Connolly, editor, the History of the Present slavery/archive issue (2016); “A Violent and Violating Archive” (2017).

proposed_edges.relationship: Dispossessed Lives (2016) studies the production of archival silence and changes the narrative gaze toward enslaved women, while refusing a claim of complete recovery.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The publisher-authorized book excerpt and interview, read, support the method; the 2010 abstract supplies an earlier distinct challenge to triumphalist representations of Polgreen. The whole book remains unread; unnamed objections are Fuentes’s report, not independently read replies.

proposed_edges.relationship: With Deborah Gray White and a collective of researchers, Scarlet and Black (2016) brings Rutgers’s involvement in slavery and dispossession into the university’s public history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher description and contents, read, establish a jointly edited committee publication with separately named chapter authors. White wrote its introduction; Fuentes is neither sole author nor sole discoverer. Contribution is scoped to this collaborative publication and stated public purpose, not a general claim to founding public history.

proposed_edges.relationship: Hartman’s “Venus in Two Acts” is explicitly named as inspiration for Connolly and Fuentes’s 2016 slavery/archive special issue, as Fuentes reports in 2017.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fuentes’s AAIHS essay explicitly identifies Hartman’s essay as inspiration. Fuentes’s author bibliography establishes Connolly’s coeditorship and 2016; USF corroborates their joint introduction in Fall 2016. Influence is limited to that collaborative project, not Hartman as sole source of Fuentes’s work or agreement on every method. The full issue remains unread.
